paper_metadata.title: Research on Domain-Specific Knowledge Graph Based on the RoBERTa-wwm-ext Pretraining Model
paper_metadata.abstract: The study addresses domain-specific knowledge graph construction from information to knowledge. It proposes a deep-learning approach using RoBERTa-wwm-ext to extract entities and relationships from open-source intelligence, together with a knowledge-fusion framework based on longest-common-attribute entity alignment, text-similarity algorithms, and classification algorithms. The named entity recognition model reaches an overall F1 of 83.07%; the RoBERTa-wwm-ext relation extraction model improves over recurrent-neural-network models by approximately 20%–30%; and longest-common-subsequence attribute similarity produces the best entity-alignment results overall.

problem_addressed: The paper seeks an effective and reliable way to construct a domain-specific military knowledge graph from heterogeneous, largely unstructured open-source intelligence, addressing ambiguity, limited data, difficult entity linking, knowledge redundancy, and the need to fuse newly extracted knowledge with existing knowledge bases.

methodology.description: The method is a sequential military Text-to-KG pipeline. Open-source military news and related semi-structured sources are collected, cleaned, and manually annotated. RoBERTa-wwm-ext encodes Chinese text; a BiLSTM-CRF performs BIO named-entity recognition; and a RoBERTa-wwm-ext plus fully connected softmax classifier predicts relations for entity pairs. Extracted knowledge is organized into ontology-compatible triples, matched with external knowledge bases, filtered into candidate entity pairs, aligned using longest-common-attribute similarity and a binary classifier, merged, stored in Neo4j, and visualized. A second fusion stage supports knowledge expansion and updating.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The paper defines a military ontology with nine entity types—country, aircraft, ship, missile, water area, aircraft carrier, military base, radar, and island—and five relation labels: country, collaboration, activity, equipment, and NULL. External data are manually ontology-matched and entity-classified before fusion.

text_to_kg_stages: Text preprocessing: collection and cleaning of open-source military text
Entity resolution and linking through paired entity alignment
Knowledge fusion and deduplication through attribute merging

input_output.input_type: Unstructured Chinese military-intelligence text, mainly open-source military news, military forums, and military sections of news platforms; external structured and semi-structured military knowledge-base data are also used for fusion.
input_output.input_granularity: Sentence-level text for named-entity recognition and relation extraction; entity pairs with attribute triples for entity alignment.
input_output.output_representation: Typed entities, classified relations, knowledge triples, aligned/merged entities, and a military knowledge graph stored in a Neo4j database and visualized.

models_and_tools: Fully connected layer and softmax relation classifier
datasets: Named-entity recognition dataset: manually annotated military-intelligence text with 9 entity types, 53,295 entity labels, and 14 MB of text; training size 10.3 MB and test size 3.2 MB
Relation-extraction dataset: 2,251 examples with five relation labels; 1,800 training examples and 451 test examples

Entity-alignment dataset: 2,648 entity pairs, constructed from 1,324 prealigned pairs and negative sampling; 28,447 attribute triples; data from an open-source military weapon/equipment knowledge graph and a weapons encyclopedia
External sources: OpenKG.CN, the Heilongjiang University military knowledge base, Weapon Encyclopedia, and Wikipedia

baselines: Edit distance + SVM/decision tree/logistic regression/naive Bayes
BERT word embedding + SVM/decision tree/logistic regression/naive Bayes
evaluation.setting: Separate test-set evaluations were conducted for named-entity recognition and relation extraction, with precision/recall/F1 comparisons against neural and BERT-family baselines. Entity alignment was evaluated on 2,648 balanced positive/negative entity pairs using combinations of four similarity methods and four classifiers. The paper reports no cross-domain evaluation, ablation study, statistical significance test, or end-to-end graph-quality evaluation.

value: RoBERTa-wwm-ext + BiLSTM + CRF achieved overall named-entity recognition precision 81.11%, recall 85.13%, and F1 83.07% (Table 9).
The named-entity recognition model had highly variable per-label F1: NAT 89.68%, PLA 77.55%, VES 68.07%, MIS 55.26%, WAT 63.52%, AIR 57.44%, BAS 49.50%, RAD 49.75%, and ISL 62.72% (Table 8).

RoBERTa-wwm-ext relation extraction achieved overall precision 97.32%, recall 97.87%, and F1 97.57% (Tables 10 and 11). BERT-wwm-ext was higher at F1 98.13%, while BiGRU-ATT and BiLSTM-ATT scored 75.74% and 67.47%, respectively (Table 11).
For entity alignment, LCS plus logistic regression achieved the best reported result: precision 99.80%, recall 99.81%, and F1 99.81% (Table 12).

The paper reports that the RoBERTa-based relation extractor improves over recurrent-neural-network baselines by approximately 20%–30%, but this comparison spans the reported models and datasets within the paper and is not independently normalized across external studies.

value: The pipeline covers both knowledge extraction and knowledge fusion, whereas the paper characterizes much prior military-domain work as concentrating mainly on extraction.
The transformer encoder supplies contextual text representations to both entity and relation extraction components.
The explicitly defined military ontology and relation inventory make the extraction task schema-guided and operationally connected to graph construction.
The alignment comparison systematically tests four similarity functions against four classifiers rather than reporting only one fusion configuration.
Review-level interpretation: the modular pipeline is comparatively easy to diagnose because extraction and alignment are evaluated separately.

RoBERTa-wwm-ext ... obtain[s] text vectors with semantic features and encode[s] the text.

value: Named-entity performance is poor for several minority entity types, including BAS F1 49.50%, RAD F1 49.75%, MIS F1 55.26%, and AIR F1 57.44%.
The data are manually annotated, increasing labor cost and limiting scalability.
The relation inventory contains only five labels, which the authors note may inflate the experimental effect and limits coverage of military relations.
The entity-alignment framework requires extensive pairwise attribute-similarity computation and therefore has low computational efficiency.

Review-level interpretation: the study evaluates component extraction and pair alignment, but does not report end-to-end graph completeness, correctness, downstream utility, or generalization to another military subdomain.

value: Manual annotation of the named-entity and relation-extraction datasets incurs substantial labor cost.
Some entity labels have poor recognition because their annotated data are scarce and the label distribution is unbalanced.
The knowledge-fusion stage has low computational efficiency because many attribute-text similarities must be calculated.
The relation dataset contains relatively few relationship types, which may make the experimental effect appear high.

value: Use semi-automatic annotation: annotate a small set of correct seed data and iteratively label more data.
Increase and rebalance the entity-label datasets and improve the model architecture and training data.
Increase the number of relation types to test the model more thoroughly.
Add a domain synonym dictionary and stop-word dictionary to reduce text-similarity calculations and improve fusion efficiency.

value: How to obtain scalable, less labor-intensive annotation for low-resource military entities and relations remains unresolved.
How to improve recognition of rare and imbalanced entity types remains unresolved.
How to extend the relation ontology beyond five labels without losing reliability remains unresolved.
How to reduce the computational cost of large-scale attribute-based entity alignment remains unresolved.
Review-level inference: the paper leaves open whether the modular system can maintain high accuracy when applied to new military sources, domains, or heterogeneous graph schemas.
